terra.problem: The passage reports a famine but does not say the family's pantry was bare.
Comparing a famine to running out of cookie dough makes light of the family's hardship, and the comparison does not land as a joke.
The claim that Edom and Moab are both neighbors of Israel has no reference.
The joke uses the book's title and the way Scripture is written as its setup.
The text reports the famine and the family's move but does not explicitly say the famine drove them out.
The statement that there was no king yet is not established by Ruth 1:1, which says the judges ruled.
The comparison to guests being too polite to leave does not match Naomi sending her daughters-in-law home and trivializes the moment.
The passage does not establish that they have left Moab, so it does not say they must head back to Moab.
Naomi's heart being in pain is presented as a fact rather than Papa's impression.
The text does not say the women looked right at Naomi.
Calling Naomi's send-off a polite exit speech makes a painful family parting sound like a social formality.
The passage does not say Naomi is returning to Judah for good, or state that neither daughter-in-law wants to let her go alone.
The text does not specify a twenty-year wait. The explanation presents that invented interval as the math of Naomi's question.
Ruth 1:11-13 does not identify a custom of a brother marrying his deceased brother's widow, and it does not say the wait would take decades.
The text does not establish that the people of Judah had not turned against Naomi; it simply does not give that as her reason.
Living in Moab for about ten years does not support the implied conclusion that its people could not have turned against Naomi.
A warm chocolate chip sticking to an apron is an awkward image for Ruth clinging to Naomi; the joke does not click.
The text does not establish that Orpah takes a road back to Moab; it does not say where on the journey the parting occurs.
Naomi testing whether Ruth means business is an invented reason for her words.
The text does not say Naomi speaks because she wants to be sure Ruth knows what she is choosing.
The passage does not say Ruth previously worshiped Moab's gods or that she is leaving those gods behind.
Ruth promises to go where Naomi goes, but the passage does not establish that there will never be any distance between them or that Ruth stays physically beside her to the end.
The claim that nobody is waiting in Moab anymore goes beyond what the passage says.
Ruth 1:4 does not establish that Naomi's entire absence from Bethlehem was about ten years. The explanation also invents why the town was stirred.
The passage does not establish that exactly ten years passed between Naomi leaving Bethlehem and returning.
The text says the whole town was stirred and gives the women's question. It does not say all eyes were on Naomi or that everyone was stunned.

The quotation combines separate pieces of dialogue with three periods and omits the comma after Naomi. Bible quotations must retain exact BSB wording and punctuation, with an ellipsis marking omitted material.
Mentioning that Leah's name will appear later in Ruth gives away a detail from a later part of the story.
Saying the next part of the story walks into the fields gives away what happens next.
The passage does not say Naomi and Ruth were hungry.
The reference to wheat harvest appearing later gives away a detail from a later part of the story.
An empty pantry stretches the text's statement that there was a famine; it does not say there was no food.

explanations.explanation: You got it, baker! When the famine hits, this man from Bethlehem packs up his wife and his two sons and goes to reside in the land of Moab (Ruth 1:1). That is a huge move when the pantry is bare. Imagine loading up the whole house because your kitchen is out of cookie dough.

Good guess, friend, because Abraham went down to Egypt during a famine (Genesis 12:10). In this story, though, the family leaves Bethlehem to go reside in the land of Moab (Ruth 1:1). You had the right idea with a famine road trip, just a different direction on the map!

Not Edom this time, baker. Ruth 1:1 tells us this man from Bethlehem takes his wife and two sons to reside in the land of Moab. Edom and Moab are both neighbors to Israel, so it is like reaching for the chocolate chips and grabbing the raisins by mistake.

There she is! Ruth 1:4 says Naomi's sons marry Moabite women, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth. When your name is on the front of the whole book, you know you are going to be important. That is like having your name carved right into the handle, the way the Millers carved Dorin into mine!

Rachel is a famous Bible name, friend, since she was Jacob's wife back in Genesis 29:28. Here in Moab, though, the two women are named Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Same letter R, different branch of the story!

Dinah was Jacob and Leah's daughter way back in Genesis 30:21. In Ruth 1:4, the Moabite wives are named Orpah and Ruth. Keep Ruth's name tucked in your apron pocket, baker, because we are going to see a lot of her.

That is what happens, friend. Ruth 1:5 tells us that both Mahlon and Chilion also die, and Naomi is left without her two sons and without her husband. That is a heavy load of grief for one person to carry. My heart really goes out to her here.

explanations.answer: Her house in Moab burns down
explanations.explanation: Nothing about a fire here, baker. The heartbreak in Ruth 1:5 is about her family: both Mahlon and Chilion also die, leaving Naomi without her two sons and without her husband. It is a very sad turn in her life.

explanations.answer: She falls sick and loses her sight
explanations.explanation: Naomi does not lose her sight here, friend. What happens in Ruth 1:5 is that both of her sons, Mahlon and Chilion, also die. She is left without her two sons and without her husband, and that is a heavy thing to walk through.

Yes indeed! Ruth 1:6 says Naomi hears in Moab that the LORD has attended to His people by providing them with food. A famine drove them out in Ruth 1:1, and now food is back on the table. When you hear the ovens are warm back home, you start packing your bags!

No king yet, baker, because Ruth 1:1 says this is back in the days when the judges ruled. What Naomi hears in Ruth 1:6 is that the LORD has attended to His people by providing them with food. After a famine, that is the exact headline you want to read!

There is no battle in this chapter, friend. The trouble back in Ruth 1:1 was a famine, so the big news in Ruth 1:6 is that the LORD has provided His people with food. Nothing turns a trip around faster than hearing the kitchen is open again!

explanations.answer: Go back to their mothers' homes
explanations.explanation: Spot on, friend. In Ruth 1:8, Naomi tells her two daughters-in-law, "Go back, each of you to your mother's home." Have you ever tried to leave a friend's house when both of you are too polite to let the other go first? Naomi is stopping right there in the road to send them back.

explanations.answer: Walk faster to beat the dark
explanations.explanation: She is not rushing them down the highway, baker. In fact, she is trying to stop them from coming at all! In Ruth 1:8, Naomi says, "Go back, each of you to your mother's home." She wants them to turn around and head back to Moab.

explanations.answer: Stay close to her the whole way
explanations.explanation: It is actually the exact opposite, friend. Instead of asking them to stick with her, Naomi tells them in Ruth 1:8, "Go back, each of you to your mother's home." She is trying to release them so they can go back to their own families.

You nailed it, baker. In Ruth 1:9, Naomi says, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband." I think that shows how much she cares about their future, even when her own heart is aching. She wants them settled and cared for.

She really does say that, friend! Right in Ruth 1:9, Naomi tells them, "May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband." She is not holding on to them for herself. She is asking the LORD to give both of them a fresh start.

explanations.answer: We will return with you to your people
explanations.explanation: That is what they say! Through their tears in Ruth 1:10, both women tell her, "Surely we will return with you to your people." Naomi just gave them the polite exit speech, and they looked right at her and said nope, we are still coming. That is some serious loyalty right there.

explanations.answer: We will stay in Moab and wait for you
explanations.explanation: Naomi isn't planning a round trip, baker, she is moving back to Judah for good (Ruth 1:7). And in Ruth 1:10, Orpah and Ruth tell her, "Surely we will return with you to your people." At this point on the road, neither one of them wants to let her go alone.

explanations.answer: We will come visit you in Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: They are talking about a lot more than a holiday visit, friend. In Ruth 1:10, they tell Naomi, "Surely we will return with you to your people." Both daughters-in-law are ready to pack it in and move all the way to Judah with her.

explanations.answer: Would you wait for them to grow up
explanations.explanation: Look at you go, baker! In Ruth 1:13, Naomi asks them, "would you wait for them to grow up? Would you refrain from having husbands?" Think about that math: waiting twenty years for a brand-new baby to be ready for a wedding! Even my timer doesn't count that high, friend.

explanations.answer: Would you raise them as your own
explanations.explanation: Naomi isn't asking for babysitters here, friend. In Ruth 1:11-13, she is talking about the custom of a brother marrying his dead brother's widow, and she asks, "would you wait for them to grow up?" Waiting for a newborn to reach wedding age would take decades!

explanations.answer: Would you go ahead to Bethlehem
explanations.explanation: She is still trying to talk them out of Bethlehem altogether, baker. In Ruth 1:13, she asks, "would you wait for them to grow up? Would you refrain from having husbands?" She is pointing out that waiting around for hypothetical baby brothers to grow into husbands makes no sense at all.

explanations.answer: The LORD's hand has turned against her
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. In Ruth 1:13, Naomi says it is much more bitter for her than for them, "because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." She is speaking straight from a bruised heart after losing her husband and both sons.

explanations.answer: The people of Judah have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The folks back in Judah haven't turned against her, baker. In Ruth 1:13, Naomi says it is much more bitter for her "because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me." That is how she sees all the loss she has been through.

explanations.answer: The people of Moab have turned against her
explanations.explanation: The text never says the Moabites turned against her, friend. After all, she lived there about ten years (Ruth 1:4). In Ruth 1:13, Naomi says the bitterness is "because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me."
That is true, baker. Ruth 1:14 says they wept aloud again, and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye. Naomi had urged them twice to go home with her blessing, and Orpah takes that tearful goodbye.

She really does kiss her goodbye, friend. Ruth 1:14 says, "Again they wept aloud, and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her." One daughter-in-law heads back the way Naomi asked, and the other holds tight.
Hold the mixer, baker! Orpah heads back, "but Ruth clung to her" (Ruth 1:14). Ruth is holding on to Naomi like a warm chocolate chip sticks to your apron. She is not going anywhere!
Right you are, friend! Ruth 1:14 tells us that Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, "but Ruth clung to her." Orpah takes the road back to Moab, and Ruth holds fast to Naomi.

You got it, baker. In Ruth 1:15, Naomi says, "Look, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home." That is attempt number THREE from Naomi! She is really testing whether Ruth means business.

Naomi really does give it one more try, friend. In Ruth 1:15, she points to Orpah leaving and tells Ruth, "follow her back home." Even with Ruth clinging to her, Naomi wants to be sure Ruth knows what she is choosing.

explanations.answer: Naomi's God will be her God
explanations.explanation: Look at that promise, friend! In Ruth 1:16, Ruth says, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." Naomi just told her Orpah went back to her gods in verse 15, and Ruth answers by choosing Naomi's God for good. That is a whole life turning around in one sentence.

explanations.answer: She will take care of Naomi's house
explanations.explanation: It goes way deeper than housework, baker. In Ruth 1:16, Ruth tells Naomi, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." She is leaving Moab's gods behind and taking the LORD as her own God.

explanations.answer: She will learn all the ways of Judah
explanations.explanation: Ruth goes straight to the heart of it in Ruth 1:16: "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." She isn't just picking up new customs. She is claiming Naomi's people and Naomi's God as her own.

That is the word, baker. In Ruth 1:17, Ruth says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me." Notice she even uses the LORD's name to seal her promise! She is locked in for life.

There won't be any distance between them if Ruth has anything to say about it, friend! In Ruth 1:16 she promised to go wherever Naomi goes, and in Ruth 1:17 she says may the LORD punish her if anything but death separates them. She is staying right by Naomi's side to the very end.
Not marriage, baker. In Ruth 1:17, Ruth says, "May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me." Where Naomi dies, Ruth plans to die and be buried too.

explanations.answer: She stops trying to persuade her
explanations.explanation: You nailed it, friend. Ruth 1:18 says when Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her. You know that moment when someone looks at you and you realize arguing is just wasting good breath? Naomi knows when she is beat!

explanations.answer: She sends her back after Orpah
explanations.explanation: Naomi already tried that line in Ruth 1:15, and Ruth shut it right down! By Ruth 1:18, when Naomi sees that Ruth is determined to go with her, she stops trying to persuade her. There is no turning Ruth around now.

explanations.answer: She tells her to wait in Moab
explanations.explanation: Nobody is waiting in Moab anymore, baker. Once Ruth makes that promise, Ruth 1:18 says Naomi sees how determined she is and stops trying to persuade her. The two of them walk on to Bethlehem together (Ruth 1:19).

That is the line, baker! In Ruth 1:19, the whole town is stirred and the women exclaim, "Can this be Naomi?" She has been gone in Moab for about ten years (Ruth 1:4), and she left with a husband and two sons. Walking back in like this has the whole town talking.

They don't ask that out loud in the verse, friend. When Naomi and Ruth walk in, Ruth 1:19 says the women of the town exclaim, "Can this be Naomi?" Ten years and a lot of heartbreak have passed since Bethlehem last saw her.
Even with Ruth right there beside her, all eyes are on the woman who left town years ago. In Ruth 1:19, the women of Bethlehem exclaim, "Can this be Naomi?" Everyone is stunned to see her back.

You got it, friend. In Ruth 1:20, she tells them, "Do not call me Naomi... Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me." In Easton's Bible Dictionary, Naomi means pleasant and Mara means bitter, so she is asking for a name that matches the pain she is carrying.

Hannah is another woman in Scripture who knew deep sorrow before Samuel was born (1 Samuel 1:10, 20). Here in Ruth 1:20, though, Naomi says, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me." Mara means bitter, and that is how her life feels that day.

Leah is from way back in Genesis 29:16, though we will hear her name in the book of Ruth before the whole story is over (Ruth 4:11)! Right here in Ruth 1:20, Naomi tells the women, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me."

Flip that cookie over, baker! You have the two words switched around. In Ruth 1:21, Naomi says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty." She left Bethlehem with a husband and two sons, and she comes back a widow.

Sharp eyes, friend! The question flipped her words backwards. In Ruth 1:21, Naomi says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty." She left with a full house of family and came home without her husband and sons.

Yes indeed, baker! Ruth 1:22 says they arrive in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest. The chapter started with a famine in Ruth 1:1, and it ends with fresh barley ready in the fields. Keep that barley harvest in mind, because the next part of the story walks right into those fields!

Close, friend, because wheat harvest does show up later in Ruth 2:23! Right when they walk into Bethlehem in Ruth 1:22, though, it is the beginning of the barley harvest. Barley comes first, and the timing could not be better for two hungry widows.

Not olives this time, baker. Ruth 1:22 tells us Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest. Chapter 1 opened with an empty pantry in a famine, and it closes with grain in the fields!
